Here you see how healthy your companies, the banks, the government and the world are. If a sector falls, it drags down its suppliers, the banks that lent to it and the people who work in it: that is how a crisis spreads.
On September 15, 2008 the investment bank Lehman Brothers went bankrupt. In 2009 the world economy shrank for the first time since World War II.
In the 1994–1995 crisis (the «tequila effect») Mexico's GDP fell about 6 % in 1995, and the crisis spread to other Latin American markets.
The Asian crisis began on July 2, 1997, when Thailand let its currency float. It spread to Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia, and Indonesia's GDP fell more than 13 % in 1998.
After the 2008 crisis, unemployment in the United States reached 10 % in October 2009.
The Basel III rules require banks to hold high-quality capital of at least 7 % of their risk-weighted assets (4.5 % minimum plus a 2.5 % buffer).
In the United States deposit insurance covers up to 250,000 dollars per person at each bank. In Mexico the IPAB covers up to 400,000 UDIS.
A bank is «systemic» when its failure would drag down the whole financial system. That is why the world's largest are required to hold more capital.
The risk that the fall of a company, a bank or a sector drags down the whole economic system, because they are all connected by loans, sales and jobs.
